explain.say: Your brain needs a steady supply of sugar, all day and all night. But you only eat a few times a day! So how does your blood sugar stay just right? Let's go round the cycle.

explain.say: Start at the top: after a meal of rice, bread or fruit, glucose floods into your blood. Your pancreas notices and releases a hormone called insulin. Think of insulin as a key that unlocks cells to let glucose in. What happens to blood sugar now?

stages.label: Glucose released
stages.note: Liver turns glycogen back to glucose

explain.say: Now look at the next stage. Insulin also tells your liver and muscles to store spare glucose as glycogen, a sort of packed sugar store. So your blood sugar drops back to normal. Where is your sugar store kept?

explain.say: Hours later, or after running about, blood sugar falls. See this stage? The pancreas releases a different hormone, glucagon, and the liver turns glycogen back into glucose. Can you see how the two hormones balance each other?

explain.say: That balancing is called negative feedback. In diabetes, insulin is missing or does not work well, so sugar stays too high. Great work! Tip: glycogen is the store; glucagon is the hormone that empties it.

faq.q: How does insulin control blood sugar?
faq.a: When blood glucose is high, the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin makes body cells take in glucose and tells the liver and muscles to store it as glycogen, so the level falls.
Glycogen is a large, insoluble store of glucose kept in the liver and muscles. It can be broken back into glucose when needed.
When blood glucose is low, the pancreas releases glucagon. It tells the liver to break glycogen down into glucose and release it into the blood, so the level rises.
Negative feedback is when a change triggers a response that reverses it. High sugar triggers insulin, which lowers it; low sugar triggers glucagon, which raises it.
asks: How does the body keep things steady?

faq.a: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so people need insulin injections or pumps. In type 2 diabetes the body's cells stop responding well to insulin; it is often managed with diet, exercise and medicine.
asks: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?

facts: Insulin and glucagon are both made by cells in the pancreas.
Glycogen is stored mainly in the liver and muscles.
